note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - New shortness of breath with wheeze and cough.
  - First noted 2–3 days ago during a run; now occurs with brisk walking. No specific trigger identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Onset 2–3 days ago; persistent since, with limited relief from salbutamol.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Denies/No report of throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change/hoarseness, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing beyond wheeze, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling, ear pain/hearing changes, neck pain/swelling.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - Known asthma; last “asthma attack” 3–4 years ago.
  - No prior hospital admissions; no prior oral steroids recalled.
  - Last asthma review ~2 years ago.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: Hay fever (allergic rhinitis). No known drug allergies.
  - Medications:
    - Salbutamol (blue inhaler) PRN; currently using daily and sometimes prophylactically (dose/frequency not documented).
    - Preventer inhaler: reported as “brown/Clenil” per clinician; patient uncertain on name earlier; uses twice daily (previously “3 puffs BID,” plan to increase to 4 puffs BID).
    - Topicals for skin: Cetraben and hydrocortisone (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Any relevant social context:
  - Physically active (running). No mention of accompaniment/supervision at home.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution:
  - None stated (no facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling reported).
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Patient-reported wheeze and exertional dyspnea; no stridor reported.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - Alert; no dizziness/syncope reported.
- Vitals and examination findings:
  - Not recorded (telehealth; no current peak flow performed; recalled “normal when well” ~380 L/min).
- Presence of another person with the patient:
  - Not stated.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression:
  - Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation in a patient with known asthma, with poor reliever response over 2–3 days. Likely contributions from exercise-induced bronchoconstriction; possible suboptimal inhaler technique/adherence.
- Evidence summary:
  - Onset during running; now dyspnea with brisk walking; wheeze and cough; no sputum; frequent salbutamol with limited benefit; atopic history (hay fever); no prior severe exacerbations or steroids.
- Differential diagnosis (aligned with transcript):
  1) Acute asthma exacerbation (high likelihood): Classic wheeze/cough/exertional dyspnea over days in known asthmatic; increased reliever need with poor relief. Opposing: lack of objective severity measures.
  2) Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (medium): Symptoms began with running and recur with exertion. Opposing: persistence beyond exercise suggests broader control issue.
  3) Poor inhaler technique/suboptimal controller use (medium): Frequent SABA with limited benefit and medication confusion; last review 2 years ago. Opposing: patient reports regular preventer use.
- Conflict noted:
  - Medication list initially mentioned “Bactroban,” later clarified to “Cetraben.”

Plan:
- Immediate actions/advice:
  - Continue salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed; may use up to every 2–4 hours temporarily while awaiting review. If needing this frequency, indicates poor control.
  - Increase preventer (brown/Clenil beclomethasone) to 4 puffs twice daily until reviewed.
  - Arrange face-to-face GP/respiratory review within the next few days for exam and peak flow.
- At in-person review:
  - Perform peak flow and oxygen saturation; chest exam.
  - Review inhaler technique and adherence; consider spacer use.
  - Consider short course of oral steroids if indicated by exam/peak flow; consider antibiotics only if bacterial infection suspected (per clinician note).
- Patient instructions:
  - Avoid known/exertional triggers until reviewed; warm-up before activity when resuming.
  - Keep reliever available; do not exceed advised frequency.
  - Remain accompanied if symptoms worsen.
- Escalation criteria/red flags (seek urgent care/A&E or call EMS):
  - Worsening breathlessness, inability to speak full sentences, cyanosis, chest tightness not relieved after repeated salbutamol, drowsiness/confusion, fainting.
  - Any new throat tightness/voice change, stridor/noisy breathing at rest, or swelling of lips/tongue/face.
- Follow-up:
  - Book face-to-face appointment as advised.
  - Schedule a comprehensive asthma review (including action plan and trigger management) given last review was ~2 years ago.
  - Consider addressing allergic rhinitis if symptomatic, as it can exacerbate asthma control.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  - Current vitals, SpO2, and lung exam; current peak flow.
  - Detailed inhaler regimen (exact drug/strength), doses, technique assessment, and spacer use.
  - Smoking status/exposures; recent illness contacts; clear trigger identification.
  - Asthma action plan on file; vaccination status (influenza/COVID-19).
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Medication list discrepancy (Bactroban vs Cetraben) — conflict noted and corrected by patient.
  - Preventer identification uncertain; clinician referenced Clenil, patient initially unsure.
● Transcript quality:
  - Minor audio/clarity issues and interruptions; some medication names unclear.
